ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Powers to DGCA 
*361. SHRI C. PERUMAL: Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION be 
pleased to state:- 
(a) whether Government have proposed to give more teeth to the 
Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA); 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION 
(SHRI PRAFUL PATEL): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the 
House. 
2 

[22 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
Statement 
(a) The powers of Directorate General of Civil Aviation are reviewed from time 
to time to keep them in consonance with international aviation requirement 
and powers are delegated, amendment in  the Aircraft Act/ Rules are carried 
out accordingly. 
(b) While powers have been delegated to DGCA in recent times relating to 
licensing of airports, grant of extension to foreign pilots and engineers, 
relaxation of statutory time limit for issuance of pilots' license, stay of foreign 
aircraft in India, change in name of ai rcraft etc., amendment in Aircraft Act is 
proposed to, inter-alia, empower DGCA to license personnel engaged in Air 
Traffic Control, certification, inspection and regulation of communication, 
notification and surveillance/air traffic management, impose penalty for 
contravention of the provisions of Chicago Convention. 
(c) Does not arise. 
SHRI C. PERUMAL: Sir, my first supplementary is this, Whether it is 
proposed to set up an airlines regulatory authority or to convert the existing DGCA 
into a full-fledged authority by including matters relating to regulation of flight 
schedule, flight safety, etc. And, if it is proposed to set up a separate 
authority, by when it is going to be set up. 
SHRI PRAFUL PATEL: Sir, the DGCA itself is a regulatory authority 
having enough teeth. But, we want to strengthen it further in view of 
expanding civil aviation sector. For information of the hon. Member, I would 
say that we had appointed Kaw Committee sometime in 2005. We received the 
Report of the Committee. Many experts were there on the Committee. All the 
issues, which he has precisely mentioned, have been taken into account. In fact, 
we have also gone one step further. We have gone in for an amendment to the 
Aircraft Act. Recently, a Bill has been introduced. As soon as it becomes an 
Act as suggested by the Government, there will be a lot of powers to the DGCA 
in various sectors of the aviation activities. The Government have already 
accepted most of the Kaw Committee's recommendations. Further, on some of 
the suggestions, consultations are going on. So, broadly, we do share the 
concern of the hon. Member and the DGCA, with all this additional powers, will be 
competent enough to look into various factors and aspects which the hon. 
Member has mentioned. 
SHRI C. PERUMAL: Sir, my second supplementary is this. Are there any 
recommendations of the Kaw Committee that have not been accepted? 
3 

RAJYA SABHA [22 August, 2006] 
If so, the reasons thereof. I will also like to know whether foreign pilots are being 
engaged indiscriminately because of the shortage of pilots in the country. It 
'yes', are the security aspects being taken into consideration? What has been 
done to recruit pilots domestically? 
SHRI PRAFUL PATEL: Sir, there were around 276 recommendations of the 
Kaw Committee. Out of which, 157 recommendations are to be implemented 
by the DGCA and the Ministry. These have broadly been accepted for 
implementation. Sixty-two recommendations required further examination. The 
Ministry and the DGCA are doing so. Fifty-four recommendations are such 
where we need consultation with other Ministries also. So, broadly on the 
point that the hon. Memebr is making, I think, the Kaw Committee's 
recommendations have been very useful and helpful. We would like to see them 
being implemented at the earliest. So far as engaging foreign pilots is 
concerned, we all know there is shortage of pilots in the country because the 
civil aviation sector has expanded very rapidly. In fact, this year, for the 
information of the hon. Members, there was roughly 50 per cent growth in the 
domestic sector. And, this trend is likely to continue. For the time being, 
because of the shortage of pilots in the country, foreign pilots are being 
recruited by different airlines. But only after all the requirements of the DGCA 
and the security agencies are met can an y foreign pilot operate in the Indian 
skies. 
SHRI CHITTABRATA MAJUMDAR: Sir, a number of private airlines are 
flying in the Indian skies. Keeping in view the prevailing terrorism, I would 
like to know whether any power has been delegated to the Director General of 
Civil Aviation to look after the security measures of the airports. 
SHRI PRAFUL PATEL: Sir, the security perse function of any airport, the 
DGCA has overriding powers over a lot of issues. There is no dispute about that. 
But, when it comes purely to the security-related issues, there are various 
agencies, like, the Bureau of Civil Aviation Security, which broadly defines the 
guidelines of airport security and the peripheral issues; the CISF is directly and 
physically looking after the airport security; we work in consultation with the 
Ministry of Home Affairs. Even the cl earances, required for airlines or pilots 
or whatever the other things, are given only after the due process has been 
followed by the Ministry of Home Affairs and is received by us in writing. 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: Sir, it has been noticed that some of the 
foreign pilots neither know Hindi nor English. This creates a lot of problem. 
4

Loss of fuel due to delay in landing of flights 
*362. SHRI SHANTARAM LAXMAN NAIK: Will the Minister of CIVIL 
AVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that commercial flight aircrafts have to hover over important 
airports like Mumbai, Delhi and Kolkata for 30 to 60 minutes both during morning and 
evening hours before landing; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the reasons therefor; and 
(c) the loss in terms of fuel, if estimated, due to the same? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION 
(SHRI PRAFUL PATEL): (a) to (c) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Due to bunching of flights, there is congestion of traffic during peak time at 
Mumbai and Delhi airports. However, there is no such congestion at Kolkata airport. 
(c) Reliable estimate with regard to loss in terms of fuel is not available. 
SHRI SHANTARAM LAXMAN NAIK: Sir, earlier, delays in flights used to be 
caused due to bad weather, incoming flight delays and technical snags, etc. Now, 
delays start at the tarmac. We hear pilots saying time and again, at Mumbai and Delhi 
Airports, that we are tenth in the queue, seventh in the queue, eighth in the queue. Then, it 
takes about 20 minutes to take off. After the take off, hovering over the sky takes 
something about 30 to 60 minutes. In this process, Sir, there can be mid-air collisions. 
When so many aircrafts are hovering around for 30 to 60 minutes, there can be mid-air 
collisions. And, if the fuel gets exhausted, even if the Control Tower wants the aircraft 
to land, it cannot give permission because there will be congestion at the airport. So, what 
steps are you taking for the purpose of minimising this congestion? 
SHRI PRAFUL PATEL: Sir, it is a fact that there is congestion during peak hours, 
especially, at Mumbai and Delhi Airports. Bulk of our aviation activities over the last 60 
or odd years have been concentrated in both these cities. The infrastructure of our 
airports, especially at the bigger airports, has been, probably, not able to match the 
growth in this sector. And, for many years, we have not been able to address this 
issue in a 
7 

RAJYA SABHA [22 August, 2006] 
time-bound manner. The next thing is, yes, there will be improvements, of course, 
once the infrastructure is upgraded. There is also another thing, and I am sure, all 
the hon; members will appreciate that in our country, as big and vast as it is, we 
need a redistribution of traffic patterns also. Everything can't be concentrated 
only in Mumbai and Delhi. It must be into the other major metros, the next level 
of metros. That is now actually happening because the pressure is so much in 
Mumbai and Delhi that redistribution of traffic is also now taking place. It is 
for the good of our country that more cities and new destinations are being linked 
by aviation. But coming to Mumbai and Delhi, yes, peak hour congestion is there. 
But I may also remind the hon. Member that peak hour congestion is there not 
only in Mumbai and Delhi, but it is a global phenomenon. All major airports 
do have more congestion than the secondary airports. Having said that, the 
Government is doing its best to see that there is an additional capacity, which is 
being created at these airports, whic h will reduce congestion. I can just 
mention about Delhi, for the time being, that Delhi has two sets of runways, 
which could not be used because there was no taxi track. One runway is to be 
used as a taxi track, and the aircrafts take off or land at the other. Now we have 
almost completed the taxi track in between the two runways. That will make it 
possible for us to operate both the runways simultaneously. The trials have 
already started. There are few hours in the morning and evening when this 
exercise is on. In the next two months, it will become more progressive; I 
would say, it will be used throughout the day. The capacity will increase by, at 
least, 25-30 per cent, to begin with, and we hope to increase it in future. That 
itself will reduce the pressures which you are mentioning right now. In terms 
of safety, I can assure you that in terms of safety standards there is no 
compromise. The Air Traffic Controlle rs are doing a good job. We are 
absolutely operating within a reasonable band of safety, as much as anywhere 
in the world, maybe, more at times. All aircrafts in today's avian age — I can 
assure all members and you must also be a little aware — operating in the Indian 
sky have TCAS, that is, Traffic Collision Avoidance System. These systems 
are, virtually, fullproof. Every aircraft knows which is the aircraft flying within 
the vicinity, at what altitude, etc. If there is a possibility of two aircrafts coming on 
the same path and colliding with each oth^r, warnings will immediately go to both 
the aircrafts, one to go up and the other to go down. So, as long as the pilot follows 
instructions, there cannot be any such possibility. I do not want to give any 
certificate of safety to anybody, but I am saying that these are the systems, 
which are in place. Therefore, there is no question, in a reasonable way, that

*366. SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that some variations in rates of VAT between State-
to-State still exist due to some of the decisions taken by the Empowered

rates in some of the States;

approved rate structure;

(e) what action the Ministry is taking or proposed to take to persuade the 
States to follow the EC approved VAT structure? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) and (b) 
The State VAT, being a tax on sale or purchase of goods within a State, is 
26 

[22 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
a State subject by virtue of Entry 54 of State List of the Constitution of India. 
An Empowered Committee of State Finance Ministers(EC) has been 
constituted to deliberate upon and decide all matters concerning State VAT. 
The EC has decided the design of VAT (including the structure of tax rates) to be 
adopted by the States. However, some variations exist in tax rates from State to 
State due to some of the EC decisions. For instance, 
(i) The EC has permitted each State to exempt 10 items out of the list of 
about 50 items of 'goods of local importance' finalized by the EC. The 
remaining items are to be taxed at 4%. 
(ii) The EC has permitted each State to notify its own list of industrial inputs 
(depending on the nature of usage of the item in the State 
concerned) which are subjected to the lower rate of 4% (as against 
general rate of 12.5%). 
(iii) The States have the discretion to tax the items in exempt category at the 
rate of 4%, and the items in 4% cat egory at the rate of 12.5%, if 
they so decide. 
(c) and (d) From the information made available by the EC and the States, 
it is seen that over and above the instances cited above, some States have made 
further deviations from the EC approved rates in respect of some items of goods. 
These States/UTs include Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Chandigarh, Delhi, 
Goa, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Kerala, Karnataka, Maharashtra, 
Meghalaya and Orissa, with Kerala having introduced a new upper rate of 20% 
on selected products recently, reflecting the particular compulsions prevailing in 
individual States. The EC has the task of closely monitoring the position in its 
meetings, in order to ensure that all the States/UTs adopt the uniform tax 
structure finalized by the EC. 
(e) The Finance Minister has met the EC on several occasions and, more 
frequently, its Chairman. Advisor to th e Finance Minister, as a permanent 
invitee to the EC, participates in EC meetings. Other senior officers of Ministry 
of Finance also attend EC meetings. However, since State VAT is a State 
subject, it is for the States to take necessary steps to follow the uniform tax 
structure collectively finalised by them.

Erosion of Ganga and its tributaries 
*373. SHRI MUKUL ROY: Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Farakka Barrage Authority is mainly responsible for the 
serious and continuous erosion by the Ganga and its tributaries like Mahananda, 
Fodhar, etc., in the districts of Malda and Murshidabad during the last three to four 
years; 
(b) how much fund has been released by the Central Government and actually 
utilized by the Farakka Barrage Authority (F.B.R) during the last three years 
for erosion-protection work; and 
(c) what are the plans for rehabilitation of the families who have lost their 
homes and lands due to the erosion? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (PROF. SAlF-UD-DIN SOZ): (a) 
No, Sir. The Farakka Barrage Project was constructed in 1975 mainly to ensure 
availability of water to Calcutta port for its navigability. Anti-erosion works 
required in the vicinity of barrage from 11.5 km in upstream and 6.9 km in the 
downstream of barrage were initially carried out by the Farakka Barrage 
Project. 
Flood Management being within the purview of the State Government, the 
Government of West Bengal is responsible for anti-erosion measures on all 
rivers in the State of West Bengal in cluding Ganga and Fodhar (Fulahar). 
However, on the^concurrence of Government of West Bengal, the jurisdiction of 
FBP was extended in 2005 for execution of anti-erosion works in the 40 km 
upstream and 80 km downstream of the barrage. Accordingly, anti-erosion 
works have been undertaken by FBP in the extended jurisdiction on river 
Ganga and Fodhar (Fulahar). 
(b) An amount of Rs. 71.00 crore was released for the period 2003-04 to 
2005-06 to Farakka Barrage Project by Ministry of Water Resources out of 
which Rs. 53.60 crore has been utilized up to March, 2006 towards execution of 
anti-erosion works in Murshidabad and Malda districts. 
(c) Farakka Barrage Project has not been assigned the works of 
rehabilitation of the families who lost their homes and lands due to erosion. This 
fails within the purview of State Government.

Common currency unit of ASEAN Countries 
*374. SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: Will the Minister of FINANCE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are likely to step up efforts to join the league of 
ASEAN countries that are working on a plan to evolve a common currency 
unit; 
(b) if so, whether India has been kept out of the plan of common currency 
unit; 
(G) if so, what are the reasons and what  steps Government are considering 
to be included in the formation of common currency unit; 
(d) to what extent the country has been successful; and 
(e) whether any final decision has been taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) to (e) 
According to some reports, an Asian Currency Unit (ACU) will be steered by 
ASEAN+3 countries as a yardstick to me asure variations in currency values. 
The ACU would help to monitor both the collective movement of Asian 
currencies against major currencies, su ch as the US dollar and the Euro, as 
well as the individual movement of each Asian currency against the regional 
average represented by the ACU. 
The ACU is likely to be based on the currencies of the 13 countries 
including members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Singapore, 
Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, the Ph ilippines, Brunei, Laos, Myanmar, 
Vietnam and Cambodia) plus Japan, China and South Korea (ASEAN+3). It 
will be a weighted average of the members' exchange rates. 
India is not a member of the ASEAN+3 and, as such, is not presently part of 
the initiative.

(b) to (d) The Archaeological Survey of India has laid down guidelines 
relating to usage of specific areas of protected monuments for holding cultural 
events. Such permission is granted to Government Departments and public 
bodies on payment of the prescribed fees as below:-

levels, etc. to ensure that no damage is caused to the monument.

Review of functioning of commodity exchanges 
2610. SHRIMATI JAYA BACHCHAN: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the number of commodity exchanges and multi-commodity 
exchanges that are in existence and functioning at present; 
(b) what is the number of notified commodities being traded by them; 
(c) whether it is a fact that these exchanges are instrumental for turning many 
businessmen as paupers because of the futures trading and have also resulted in 
the unjustified increase in the price of pulses; and 
(d) if so, whether Government propose to review their functioning, if not, the 
reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
PAWAN KUMAR BANSAL): (a) There are 24 Commodity Exchanges, which are 
recognized for commodity futures trad ing. At present, 22 Exchanges are 
functioning, and out of these, 18 Exchanges are multi-commodity Exchanges. 
(b) At present, there are 103 commodi ties notified for commodity futures 
trading, and out of these, active trading is taking place in 92 commodities. 
(c) and (d) No Sir. The commodity fu tures market performs important 
functions of price discovery and price risk management. Forward Market 
Commission (FMC), the Regulator for commodity futures market, set up under 
the provisions of the Forward Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1952, has laid down 
various regulatory measures for ensuring the orderly functioning of the commodity 
Exchanges. These regulatory measures ensure that the prices of futures contracts 
traded at the Exchanges reflect demand and supply situation of a particular 
commodity and that the Exchanges efficiently perform the function of price 
discovery, which benefits all the stakeholders, including the farmer. FMC is also 
keeping a close watch on the developments in the commodity futures market on a 
continuous basis.

Unfair means to collect debt by bank 
2613. SHRI RAJEEV CHANDRA SEKHAR: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether there have been recent reports that some people have been driven to 
suicide by the debt collection activities of a certain bank that was an erstwhile 
development bank created by Government; 
(b) whether it is a fact that goondas and criminals elements were/are used 
by this bank for such collection activities; 
(c) what steps/action Government have taken against such banks 
especially when Government are common man oriented; and 
(d) the authorities responsible for regulating Banks vis-a-vis their conduct 
towards borrowers, since activities of these banks seem to either inadvertently 
or deliberately resulting in nexus with criminal elements; and 
(e) whether there is any legislation to protect borrowers from action of 
lenders like this? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
PAWAN KUMAR BANSAL): (a) to (c) Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has come 
to know of two media reports alleging that the borrowers committed suicide 
due to the alleged harassment and humiliation by 
92 

[22 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
recovery agents of a private sector bank. In both the cases, the concerned police 
authorities are investigating the matter. 
(d) and (e) All commercial banks in the country are regulated by RBI. RBI 
had issued Fair Practices Code for Lenders in May 2003 advising scheduled 
commercial banks and All India Financial Institutions not to resort to undue 
harassment of the borrowers including credit card holders. The Indian Banks' 
Association (IBA) has formulated a "Model Code for collection of dues and 
repossession of security" as also a "Fair Practice Code for credit card operations" 
which has been recommended to banks for adoption and implementation. As per 
the Model Code, banks commit to maintaining Dignity and Respect to 
customers in their Debt Collection Policy and not follow policies that unduly 
coercive in collection of dues. The Fair Practice Code for credit cards operations 
incorporates a clause that the banks' dues collection policy would be built on 
courtesy, fair treatment and persuasion. RBI has also issued guidelines on credit 
card operations on 21.11.2005, which provide that the Banks/ NBFCs and their 
agents should not resort to intimidation or harassment of any kind, either verbal 
or physical, against any person in their debt collection efforts, including acts 
intended to humiliate poblicly or intrude the privacy of the credit card holders' 
family members, referees and friends, making threatening and anonymous 
calls or making false and misleading representations. Any violation by banks 
in this regard attracts penalties from RBI. 
The Banking Ombudsman Scheme, 2006 has been notified w.e.f. 1st 
January, 2006 enlarging the scope of the scheme to cover customer 
complaints in areas such as levying service charges without prior notice to the 
customer and non-adherence to the Fair Practices Code as adopted by the banks, 
credit card complaints, deficiency in providing the services assured by the banks 
through their agents etc.

Statement— II 
Guidelines for selection of part-time non-official Director on the Board of 
Directors of Nationalised Banks. 
The following criteria may be adopted for nomination of part-time non-
official Directors (NOD) on the Boards  of Public Sector Banks/Financial 
Institutions etc. 
(I) GENERAL 
1. Nominations will be made keeping in view the provisions of the 
relevant Acts/Rules. 
2. The suitability of nominees may be assessed in terms of formal 
qualification and expertise, track record, integrity etc. For assessing 
integrity and suitability, information on criminal records, financial 
position, civil actions, undertaken to pursue personal debts, refusal 
of admission to or expulsion from professional bodies, sanctions 
applied by regulators and similar bodies and previous questionable 
business practices etc. will be relied upon. 
3. Persons with special academic training or practical experience in the 
fields of agriculture, rural economy, banking, cooperation, economics, 
business management, human resources, finance, law, marketing 
industry and IT will ordinarily be considered. 
4. As far as possible representation may also be given to women and the 
persons belonging to SC/ST community. 
(II) EDUCATION 
1. an NOD should at least be a graduate, Educational qualifications may be 
relaxed with the approval of ACC in case of farmers, depositors 
and artisans. 
(III) AGE 
1. The age of the Director, on the date of recommendation by 
Appointments Board, should not be less than 40 years and 
preferably below 60 years. The upper age limit may be relaxed in 
case of outstanding experts, eminent persons. 
(IV) WORK EXPERIENCE 
1. Professionals/academicians should ordinarily have 10 years of work 
experience in the particular field. 
106 

[22 August. 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
(V) DISQUALIFICATION 
1. A Director already on a Bank/FI, under any category, may not be 
considered for nomination as NOD on any other Bank/FI. 
2. Persons connected with hire purchase, financing, investments, leasing 
and other para-banking activities, MPs, MLAs, MLCs, and Stock 
Brokers will not be appointed as non-official Directors 
'    on the Boards of Banks/FIs 
3. No Person may be re-nominated as a NOD on the Board of a Bank/ 
Fl on which he/she has served as Director in the past under any 
category for two terms or six years whichever is longer. 
4. An NOD would not be considered for nomination as a Director on 
the Board of a Bank/FI if such  Director has already been a 
NOD/shareholder-Director on the Board of any other Bank/FI for six 
years, whether continuously or intermitently. 
(VI) PROFESSIONAL RESTRICTION 
1. NOD will not accept/will not be allotted any work of the Bank/FI for 
two years after demitting office as Director of that Bank/FI. 
2. During his term as NOD on any Bank, such Director will not 
undertake any professional work (statutory audit, concurrent audit, 
legal retainership or empanelment as a lawyer etc.) in any other Public 
Sector Bank. 
3. If a person having professional relationship with Bank, including 
Cooperative Banks, is selected for being nominated on the Board of any 
Bank, he will have to server his connection with the Bank before such 
appointment. 
4. Professionals shall not be nominated on the Board of a PSB with 
which, they have had a business relationship during the last 3 years 
before such nominations 
(VII) REGIONAL REPRESENTATION 
Effort should be made to ensure representation of all the six zones 
of the country-North, South, East, West, Central and North-East-on the 
Boards of Public Sector Banks taken together.

banks 
2462. DR. VIJAY MALLYA: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that RBI has ordered foreign banks operating in the country 
to strictly monitor the accounts of Indian politically exposed persons and whether a copy 
of the said order be placed on the Table of the House; 
120 

[22 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) whether RBI or Government have identified such classes of persons and if 
so, the details thereof; and 
(c) what safeguards are built into the system to prevent Government to the 
genuine cases of politically exposed persons and the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
PAWAN KUMAR BANSAL): (a) to (c) Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has issued 
Know Your Customer (KYC) Guidelines—Anti Money Laundering Standards 
vide their circular dated 29th November, 2004. As per the guidelines, Politically 
Exposed Persons (PEPs) are individuals who are or have been entrusted with 
prominent public functions in a foreign country, e.g. Heads of States or of 
Governments, senior politicians, senior government/judicial/military officers, 
senior executives of state-owned corporations, important political party 
officials, etc. In terms of the KYC Guidelines, the banks should gather sufficient 
information on any person/ customer of this cetegory intending to establish a 
relationship and check all the information available on the person in the public 
domain. Banks should verify the identity of the person and seek information 
about the sources of funds before accepting the PEP as a customer. The 
decision to open an account for PEP should be taken at a senior level which should 
be clearly spelt out in Customer Acceptance policy. Banks should also subject 
such accounts to enhanced monitoring on an ongoing basis. These norms may also 
be applied to the accounts of the family or close relatives of PEPs.

Control over misuse of Participatory Notes 
2645. SHRI SANJAY RAUT: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) what steps Government are taking to control misuse of participatory notes 
as an instrument of investment in Indian Capital Market; 
(b) whether participatory notes holders disclose their identity by 
submitting constitutional documents, address proof, photo ID etc.; and 
(c) how it is ensured that investment through participatory notes is made in 
compliance with provision of Anti Money Laundering Act?

PAWAN KUMAN BANSAL): (a) and (b) In 2004, the Securities and Exchange 
Board of India (Foreign Institutional Investors) Regulations 1995 were amended to 
bring Flls issuing Participatory Notes (PNs) within the ambit of the FH 
regulations. The amendment to the regulations is intended to ensure that Flls 
issuing PNs would do so only to regulated entities. 
Also further downstream issuance, if any, would be done to regulated entities 
only. 
An appropriate reporting format has been put in place wherein Flls issuing PNs are 
required to report the same on a monthly basis. As per the format of this report, 
the following information is furnished at the end of every month:

the jurisdiction where the subscribing entity has been incorporated, 
the regulator for the jurisdiction, 
the date of issue, 
the date of maturity, 
outstanding investments at the end of each month. 
The reporting Fll also provides an undertaking which essentially states that 
PNs have not been issued to NRIs/OCBs. 
(c) The Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002 and the 
Rules made thereunder, put an obligation on the Banking Companies, 
Financial Institutions and intermediaries to submit Cash Transaction Reports 
and Suspicious Transaction Reports to curb crimes of money laundering and 
related crimes. 
SEBI has issued circulars dated 18.01.06 and 20.03.06, to all the 
intermediaries registered with SEBI, including foreign institutional investors, 
advising them to ensure that a proper policy framework on anti-money 
laundering measures is put into place within one month from the date of the

Diversioh of Kerosene from PDS 
2684. SHRI MAHENDRA MOHAN: Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND 
NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a recent survey by the National Council of Applied 
Economic Research has brought out that 38 per cent of the entire supply of kerosene to the 
Public Distribution system, targeted for supply to the below poverty line population, is 
pilfered and sold in the black market; and 
(b) if so, the details of steps being taken to check this diversion of kerosene from 
the Public Distribution System to ensure that the targeted below poverty line population can 
avail of the assigned supplies, especially in the far flung areas of the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL 
GAS (SHRI DINSHA J. PATEL): (a) With a view to assessing the genuine demand 
requirement of kerosene in different States/UTs, the Government commissioned in 
December, 2004 a study of the subject through the National Council for Applied Economic 
Research (NCAER). NCAER in its report, submitted in October, 2005, has estimated the 
total leakage/ diversion of kerosene meant for distribution under Public Distribution System 
(PDS) as 38.6% of total sale of PDS kerosene in 2004. 
(b) Under the Control Orders issued by the Government to prevent fuel adulteration, 
under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955, State Governments are empowered 
to take action against those indulging in adulteration. Government have requested the State 
Governments/Union Territory Administrations to take steps to control adulteration and 
black-marketing. 
Effective 2nd October, 2005, Government have launched "Jan Kerosene Pariyojana" as a 
pilot project in 414 blocks covering 23 States and one Union Territory to strengthen the 
PDS kerosene distribution mechanism and control the diversion of PDS kerosene for 
adulteration. 
164 

[22 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA

the following further measures:—

external agencies;

(MS), High Speed Diesel (HSD) and Kerosene through Global 
Positioning System (GPS); 
(iii) Drawal/testing of samples by independent agencies; 
(iv) Automation of retail outlets

National tourism promotion board 
2698. SHRI SHAHID SIDDIQUI: 
SHRI KAMAL AKHTAR. 
Will the Minister of TOURISM be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Govemment propose to set up a National Tourism Promotion Board; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF TOURISM (SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI): (a) to (c) There has 
been a demand from various quarters to set up a National Tourism Promotion Board. However, 
tourism being an amalgam of various activities like accommodation, food & beverages, 
entertainment services, transportation (railways, roadways, civil aviation, waterways), 
taxes, travel agencies, etc., which fall within the jurisdiction of different Ministries or 
State Governments, pros & cons of setting up of a "Board" vis-a-vis the existing system 
need detailed examination.

2699. SHRI RUDRANARAYAN PANY:

hot-spot to boost tourism;

(b) if so, the details thereof;

for the purpose; and

financially and physically to achieve the objective? 
THE MINISTER OF TOURISM (SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI): (a) to (c) 
Development and promotion of tourism is undertaken primarily by the State Governments/UT 
Administrations. The Ministry of Tourism, Government of India, extends financial 
assistance to the State Governments/UT  Administrations for tourism related 
projects which are identified in consultation and interaction with them under 
schemes for Integrated Development of T ourists Circuits, Product/Infrastructure 
Development of Destinations and Assistance to Large Revenue Generating Projects. Project 
proposals for prioritized projects that are complete in all respect are examined under 
scheme guidelines and approved on the basis afinter-se priority and funds released subject to 
availability under respective head.

Distt. Puri and Ganjam as Tourist Destination in the year 2005-06. 
(d) Ministry of Tourism, Govt, of India had prepared a 20-year Perspective Tourism Plan for 
the State of Orissa in the year 2003 and sent to the State Government for their persuar 
and use. It contained the following recommendations: 
(i) SWOT analysis, tourist forecasts, etc. 
(ii) Suggested strategies for touris m promotion, product development, 
augmentation of infrastructure and employment potential. 
(iii) Environmental Management Plan, Investment Plan and sources of funding. 
(iv) Direct and indirect economic benefits from the Plan. 
(v) Implementation Plan containing priority projects, institutional mechanism, 
modes of private participation and marketing strategies.

Shortage of funds in Sardar Sarovar Project 
2708. PROF. ALKA BALRAM KSHATRIYA: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Sardar Sarovar Project is a multi-purpose project which 
will benefit the four States of Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Rajasthan and Gujarat by 
way of sharing of irrigation facilities and power generation; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the project is facing acute shortage of funds which is 
hampering the completion of 101 Kms. stretch of Narmada Main Canal; 
(c) whether the State have made a request to the Central Government for additional 
funds to ensure the completion of the project; and 
(d) if so, what is Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (PROF. SAIF-UD-DIN SOZ): (a) 
The Sardar Sarovar Project is an inter-state multi-purpose project on the river Narmada 
in Gujarat. It is a joint venture with sharing of irrigation and power from the project, 
among the states of Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Rajasthan and Gujarat. 
(b) to (d) At present, construction of main canal carrying water from-Sardar 
Sarovar Dam upto Rajasthan border is completed upto 357 kms length out of its total 
length of 458 kms in Gujarat. As reported by Government of Gujarat it is planned to 
complete remaining 101 kms upto Rajasthan border by October, 2006. 
Keeping in view the need to accelerate the construction of Narmada Main Canal 
and distributaries for early development of irrigation facilities in the command area of the 
project, the Government of India has decided to include Sardar Sarovar Project under 
Accelerated Irrigation Benefits Programme (AIBP). Under this Programme, 
Government of India has released Central Loan Assistance (CLA)/grant of R~s. 
4415.85 crore from the financial years 1996-97 to March, 2006, out of which Rs. 339.60 
crore was released as grant during the financial year 2005-06. 
The project or project component could be included in the programme of Central 
financial assistance on the basis of proposals submitted by the State Government and 
eligibility of project for inclusion in the programme as per eligibility criteria of the 
programme.

to (c) The Narmada Control Authority based on the clearances given by its Sub-

The Hon'ble Prime Minister in response to the reference made by the Hon'ble 
Minister (WR) and observations of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in its Order dated 
17th April, 2006 decided to constitute Sardar Sarovar Project Resettlement & Rehabilitation 
Oversight Group (OSG) headed by Shri V.K. Shunglu to verify the status of 
rehabilitation in Madhya Pradesh of the families affected by raising the height of the dam 
from EL 110.64 m to EL 121.92 m as per the approved design.

The OSG has investigated the matter and submitted its report as per the terms of 
reference to the Hon'ble Minister (WR) on 3rd July, 2006. The Hon'ble Minister (WR)

taken by the Hon'ble Prime Minister on 8th July, 2006 on the Report of OSG was 
filed in the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India along with the Report of the OSG on 10th 
July, 2006, as per the direction of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in its Order dated 
8th May, 2006 in the matter of Civil Writ Petition No. 328 of 2002. 
The Supreme Court of India heard the matter on 10th July, 2006. The Court 
directed the parties to file their response to the Report within three weeks and replies 
thereto within three weeks thereafter. The case has been listed for September, 2006. 
Meanwhile, directions have been issued to Government of Madhya Pradesh to 
expedite the works on the Resettlement and Rehabilitation sites and to take measures 
as directed by the Hon'ble Prime Minister. 
As per the order of the Hon'ble Supreme Court, raising of the height of the Sardar 
Sarovar Dam beyond 90 metres will be only pari passu with the implementation of the 
relief and rehabilitation and on the clearance by the relief and rehabilitation Sub-Group. 
As per the status of Resettlement & Rehabilitation (R&R) as on 7.4.2006, 31,500 
Project Affected Families likely to be under impact of submergence due to raising the 
dam height upto EL 121.92 m pertaining to the State of Gujarat, Maharashtra and 
Madhya Pradesh have been resettled. Out of 31,500 PAFs, 4726 families belong to 
Gujarat, 3452 families to Maharashtra and 23,322 families to Madhya Pradesh.

recharge to groundwater for conservation of water.

Recharge to Ground Water under the Chairmanship of Union Minister of Water 
Resources with the main objective to popularize the concept of artificial 
recharge to ground water among all stakeholders. The Central Ground Water 
Board has circulated Manual/Guidelines on Artificial Recharge to Ground

Development of ground water in Uttar Pradesh 
2717. SHRI LAUT SURI: W ill the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether a final decision has been taken with Japan International 
Cooperation Agency (JICA) for the development of ground water in Uttar 
Pradesh, 
(b) if so, the extent of assistane proposed to be made available by the Agency, 
the share of the State Government, if any, and that of the Central Government for 
the venture; and 
(c) the time likely to be taken for the completion of the job? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (PROF. SAIF-UD-DIN SOZ): (a) 
and (b) Yes Sir. Exchange for Notes has been signed between the 
Governments of India and Japan on 5th January, 2006 for development of ground 
water in the State of Uttar Pradesh for grant assistance of Japanese Yen 603 Million 
(Rs. 23 crore equivalent). As per the Exchange of Notes, the State Government 
shall bear all the expenses, other than those covered by the grant, necessary for 
execution of the project. 
(c) The grant assistance is to be availed from 5.1.2006 to 4.1.2007. 
Baglihar Hydro-Electric Project 
2718. SHRI T.S. BAJWA: Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES 
be pleased to state: 
(a) the estimated cost of Baglihar Hydroelectric Power Project and the time 
frame for completion of the project when it was conceived; 
(b) the details of estimated cost and the amount expended on the project till 
now; 
(c) whether there is any proposal with Government to hand over the project 
for completion to a private party; 
(d) how much more funds are required to complete the project; 
(e) whether Government have any proposal to black list any company that 
has delayed the completion of project; 
209 

RAJYA SABHA [22 August, 2006] 
(0 whether anyone has been held responsible for the delay and the action 
taken against them; and 
(g) how many Hydroelectric Power Projects have been handed over to . private 
parties? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (PROF. SAIF-UD-DIN SOZ): (a) 
and (b) The estimated cost as techno-economically cleared by Central Electricity 
Authority in March, 1985 was Rs. 608.89 crore (Net) at September 1984 price 
level, excluding the cost of transmission system. The cost was updated in 
March 1990 at February 1989 price level to Rs. 887.23 crore (Net) including 
cost of associated transmission line. The project was expected to be completed 
and implemented within six years from the date of commencement of 
construction work and a period of one and a half year had been earmarked for 
development of basic infrastructure. The State Government of J&K cleared the 
project in January 1998 at a sanctioned cost of Rs. 3810 crore. The original 
estimated cost as adopted by Power Finance Corporation is Rs. 4000 crore and 
the project was planned to be complete d by 31st December, 2004. The latest 
cost as estimated is of the tune of Rs . 4300 crore. Total expenditure incurred 
ending July 2006 is Rs. 3348.12 crore. 
(c) As informed by the Project Authority, there is no such proposal. 
(d) As per latest cost, balance of Rs. 951.88 crore is required for 
completion of the project. 
(e) As per the Project Authority, there is no such proposal. 
(f) As informed by the Project Authority, delay has been caused due to 
various reasons viz. land acquisition problem financial difficulties and 
occurrence of Force Majeure events in July-August, 2005. 
(g) As informed by Central Electri city Authority, seven hydro-electric 
projects of total installed capacity of 2061 MW are presently under 
execution in private sector.

Government for financial and technical assistance for prevention of erosion by the 
Ganga and the Padma rivers tn the district of Murshidabad;

during last 3 years (2003-04,2004-05 & 2005-06); out of which Rs. 53.60 crore 
has been utilized.

Kallada Irrigation Programme 
2721. SHRI P.R. RAJAN: Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether there is any proposal from the Competent Authority of Kerala to 
include Kallada Irrigation Programme under restructured Command Area 
Development Water Management Programme; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the present status of the proposal? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (PROF. SAIF-UD-DIN SOZ): (a) 
Yes, Sir. 
(b) Kallada Irrigation Project was considered for inclusion under the 
Command Area Development and Water Management (CADWM) 
Programme in XVI meeting of the Inter-Ministerial Sanctioning Committee held 
oh 21.4.2006. This Committee decided that State Government would submit 
revised Detailed Project Report (DPR) furnishing areas already covered under

Programme. State Government has not yet submitted the revised DPR. 
Completion of irrigation projects 
2722. SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there were 494 approved and unapproved ongoing irrigation 
projects at the beginning of Tenth Plan; 
(b) if so, whether these comprised 173 major, 235 medium and 86 
extention, renovation and modernization (ERM) spilled over from previous Plan; 
(c) whether currently there are 452 ongoing irrigation projects of which 157 
are major, 212 medium and 83 ERM; 
 
(d) if so, whether huge cost and time overruns have become a 
characteristic feature of irrigation projects; and 
(e) if so, what steps Government propose to take to complete these projects 
in the Eleventh Plan? 
212 

[22 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (PROF. SAIF-UD-DIN SOZ): (a) 
to (d) Yes sir. 
(e) Irrigation being a state subject, the irrigation projects are investigated, planned, 
formulated, executed and funded by the State Governments themselves out of their 
own resources and as per their own priorities.. Concerned with the delay in completion 
of the irrigation projects mainly due to the resource crunch being faced by the states, 
the Central Government launched the Accelerated Irrigation Benefits Programme (AIBP) in 
1996-97 to provide Central Loan Assistance (CLA) to such major/medium ongoing 
irrigation projects which are in advanced stage of construction and are beyond the 
resources capability of the States. Under the programme, CLA/Grant of Rs. 
19437.8837 crore has been provided upto March, 2006 for completion of major, medium 
and minor irrigation projects. 11th Five Year Plan is not formulated so far. 
Schemes to meet the demand of water 
2723. SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) what efforts are underway in the Ministry to cope with the increasing demand of 
water in future; and 
(b) if so, the details of the schemes which are already in existence in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (PROF. SAIF-UD-DIN SOZ): (a) 
and (b) The National Commission for Integrated Water Resources Development Plan 
in its report has projected the estimates of total annual water requirements for various 
scenarios. The estimated water requirements for the year 2010,2025 and 2050 are 710 
BCM, 843 BCM and 1180 BCM respectively. 
Several measures for developemnt and management of water resources are undertaken by 
the respective State Governments which include creation of storages, restoration of water 
bodies, rain water harvesting, artificial recharge to ground water and adoption of better 
management practices etc. State Governments conceive plan and implement major, 
medium and minor schemes, both surface and ground water for utilization of water 
resources. Storage capacity of about 213 BCM has been created so far. As per present 
assessment, the total estimated storage capacity of the various projects under 
construction is about 76 BCM. Further, the State 
213 

RAJ YA SABHA [22 August, 2006] 
Governments have identified various other schemes for investigation and planning 
and the estimated storage for such schemes is about 108 BCM. Government of 
India is providing Central assistance to the State Governments through various 
schemes/programmes, such as Accelerated Irrigation Benefits Programme (AIBP); 
Command Area Development and Water Management (CADWM) Programme; 
National Project for Repair, Renovation and Restoration of Water Bodies 
directly linked to Agriculture etc. The Government of India also encourages 
rainwater harvesting and recharge to groundwater for conservation of water. 
The Ministry of Water Resources has also formulated a National 
Perspective Plan (NPP) for water resources development envisaging inter-basin 
transfer of water from surplus basin to deficit basins/area.
